original: A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined.
draft: One named digital edition does not prove that all ancient copies agree. Other Hebrew copies were not checked.
meaningCheck: Retains the limit to one digital edition and the absence of checks of other Hebrew copies.

original: English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.
draft: English in square brackets gives the researcher’s plain translation. It is not a KJV quote or a dictionary entry.
meaningCheck: Preserves who supplied the English and both limits on its use.

original: The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text.
draft: The Hebrew quotes use the digital edition named in Sources.
meaningCheck: The full edition name remains in Sources and in sourceEditionNames; no claim about all Hebrew copies is added.

original: It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original.
draft: It is not a guide to readings across ancient copies. It does not show that all Greek copies agree or which wording came first.
meaningCheck: Retains the lack of a comparison of copies, the agreement limit, and the original-wording limit.

original: The Greek New Testament wording is Tischendorf’s eighth edition as served by bolls.life (TISCH), compared with the Textus Receptus text served there (TR); neither is a critical apparatus.
draft: The New Testament comparison uses two Greek editions served by bolls.life. Sources names both editions. Neither is a guide to readings across ancient copies.
meaningCheck: Both precise edition names and bolls.life remain in sourceEditionNames; neither edition becomes a claim about every copy.

original: The Greek quoted is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament.
draft: The Greek quotes use a printed edition of the old Greek translation of the Old Testament. Sources names that edition.
meaningCheck: Retains a printed edition within an older translation tradition, rather than treating it as all Greek copies.

original: This record does not say which reading is original, and two digital editions are not a survey of manuscripts.
draft: This record does not say which wording came first. Comparing two digital editions is not a survey of ancient copies.
meaningCheck: Retains the uncertainty about original wording and the limited basis of two digital editions.

original: The difference is between Greek editions: the Textus Receptus text served agrees with the KJV and Tischendorf’s text does not.
draft: The difference is between Greek editions. Greek edition 2 agrees with the KJV. Greek edition 1 does not.
meaningCheck: The draft Sources key maps edition 1 to Tischendorf and edition 2 to Textus Receptus; check that UI preserves this key.

original: The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament.
draft: The Greek uses a printed edition of the old Greek translation of the Old Testament. Sources names that edition.
meaningCheck: Retains the printed-edition and translation-tradition limits, with the full name kept in Sources.

original: The English quoted from Brenton’s own page is given only to show how that edition renders the Greek it prints; it is not a lexicon entry.
draft: The English on that edition’s page shows only how it translates the Greek printed there. It is not a dictionary entry.
meaningCheck: Keeps the same edition as the subject and limits the English to its own translation.

original: It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original, and the record does not claim the Greek is a mistranslation of the Hebrew.
draft: It is not a guide to readings across ancient copies. It does not show that all Greek copies agree or which wording came first. The record does not claim the Greek mistranslates the Hebrew.
meaningCheck: Preserves all three source limits and the separate refusal to call the Greek a Hebrew mistranslation.

original: The psalm is verse; the comparison is of what the texts print, not of what the singer meant beyond the words quoted.
draft: The psalm is poetry. The comparison concerns the printed words. It does not claim what the singer meant beyond the words quoted.
meaningCheck: Retains the literary form and the limit on claims about the singer’s intent.

original: The record does not say what the Hebrew words quoted mean, and does not say which Greek word corresponds to which Hebrew word.
draft: The record does not say what the quoted Hebrew words mean. It does not match individual Greek words to Hebrew words.
meaningCheck: Retains both limits: no Hebrew meaning claim and no word-by-word alignment.

original: No tag is proposed: the record compares the wording of the passages and does not rest on a difference between the KJV and the Greek.
draft: No tag is proposed. The record compares the passages’ wording. It does not rely on a difference between the KJV and the Greek.
meaningCheck: Keeps the absence of a proposed tag and the basis of the comparison.

original: Where Greek is quoted, the Textus Receptus text served carries the same words.
draft: Where Greek is quoted, Greek edition 2 carries the same words.
meaningCheck: Greek edition 2 is explicitly mapped to the served Textus Receptus text in the draft Sources key.

original: The book is a history written in prose; the comparison is of what the texts print, not of why the writer worded it so.
draft: The book presents history in prose, or ordinary writing. This comparison concerns the printed words, not why the writer chose them.
meaningCheck: Keeps the literary description and does not turn it into proof that every event happened.

original: The book is prophecy in verse and sermon; the comparison is of what the texts print, not of what the prophet meant beyond the words quoted.
draft: The book presents prophecy through poetry and sermons. The comparison concerns the printed words. It does not claim what the prophet meant beyond the words quoted.
meaningCheck: Preserves both literary forms and the limit on inferred prophetic meaning.

original: The book is prophecy in verse; the comparison is of what the texts print, not of what the prophet meant beyond the words quoted.
draft: The book presents prophecy through poetry. The comparison concerns the printed words. It does not claim what the prophet meant beyond the words quoted.
meaningCheck: Preserves poetry and the limit on inferred prophetic meaning.

original: It does not rule on whether or how the commandment applies today, and it adds no finding about the passage.
draft: It does not decide whether or how the commandment applies today. It adds no finding about the passage.
meaningCheck: Keeps both the modern-application limit and the absence of an added finding.

original: The book is prophecy and vision; the comparison is of what the texts print, not of what the prophet meant beyond the words quoted.
draft: The book presents prophecy and visions. The comparison concerns the printed words. It does not claim what the prophet meant beyond the words quoted.
meaningCheck: Retains both literary forms and the stated limit on meaning.

original: The book is verse and aphorism; the comparison is of what the texts print, not of what the writer meant beyond the words quoted.
draft: The book contains poetry and short sayings. The comparison concerns the printed words. It does not claim what the writer meant beyond the words quoted.
meaningCheck: Explains aphorisms as short sayings without expanding what the writer meant.

original: A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees, and neither edition settles which reading is earlier.
draft: One named digital edition does not prove that all ancient copies agree. Neither edition settles which wording came earlier.
meaningCheck: Keeps both the agreement and earlier-wording limits.

original: English glosses in brackets are the researcher’s plain renderings, not lexicon entries.
draft: English in brackets gives the researcher’s plain translations, not dictionary entries.
meaningCheck: Preserves the researcher attribution and distinction from a dictionary.

original: Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text.
draft: The Hebrew quotes use the digital edition named in Sources.
meaningCheck: Full edition identity remains in Sources and sourceEditionNames.

original: It does not show which wording is original.
draft: It does not show which wording came first.
meaningCheck: Keeps the limit on identifying original wording; no reading is chosen.

original: The record does not say which reading is original.
draft: The record does not say which wording came first.
meaningCheck: Preserves the absence of an original-wording judgment.
